The first cohort of Ensis directus larvae maintained at 18 °C [T = 18 °C] underwent eclosion after a brief embryonic period, with hatching occurring at just 5.0 days [ab = 5.0 days] post-fertilisation. This rapid transition from the embryonated egg stage to a free-swimming veliger larva is typical of many marine bivalves and reflects the energetic strategy of minimising the duration of yolk dependence. Following hatching, these lecithotrophic larvae began their pelagic phase, during which they underwent significant morphological development. A separate group reared under cooler conditions at 12 °C [T = 12 °C] took considerably longer to reach the metamorphic climax, with the time since birth at metamorphosis recorded as 10.5 days . This temperature sensitivity in developmental timing highlights the profound influence of thermal regime on early life-history trajectories. Upon completing metamorphosis, the newly transformed post-metamorphic juveniles were measured to have a shell length at this transition of 0.045 cm , a dimension that marks the end of planktonic vulnerability and the onset of benthic life.

Juvenile Ensis directus display a protracted period of somatic growth before attaining reproductive maturity. Under controlled laboratory conditions at 12 °C [T = 12 °C], the time since birth at puberty was determined to be 492.0 days [tp = 492.0 days], a duration that allows for substantial accumulation of somatic tissue before the onset of gametogenesis. At this critical life-history transition, the shell length at puberty was estimated at 4.841 cm [Lp = 4.841 cm], reflecting a several-hundred-fold increase in shell dimension from the metamorphic stage. The gonadosomatic index (GSI) of Ensis directus, measured at 12 °C [T = 12 °C], was 2.5% [GSI = 2.5%]. This disparity suggests that E. directus allocates a smaller proportion of its body mass to reproductive tissue at any given time, potentially favouring a more protracted or iteroparous spawning strategy. The onset of sexual maturation is thus a clearly demarcated event influenced by both thermal conditions and energetic status.

Growth of the shell continues steadily through the juvenile and adult stages, with field surveys and laboratory rearing studies providing detailed length-at-age data. Under thermal conditions of 12 °C [T = 12 °C], individuals attain a shell length of 8.0 cm  at 730 days, representing a nearly twofold increase from the length recorded at puberty. Continued accretion over the subsequent years results in a shell length of 15.0 cm  at 1825 days, indicating that growth remains substantial even after the onset of reproductive activity at a temperature of 12 °C [T = 12 °C]. The ultimate total length for this species has been reported as 17.1 cm [Li = 17.1 cm], although this value shows notable geographic variation. Populations in German waters have been documented reaching 18.6 cm, while those in the western Atlantic can attain sizes of up to 20 cm, suggesting that local environmental conditions, such as food availability and temperature, play a significant role in determining maximum attainable shell size. The species thus exhibits considerable plasticity in its asymptotic dimensions.

Suspension feeding in Ensis directus underpins all energetic investment in growth and reproduction, and the species' filtering capacity has been quantified under controlled temperatures. At 12 °C [T = 12 °C], the maximum specific filtering rate was measured at 5.3 L/h , a value that illustrates the substantial water-processing capability of this bivalve. This rate allows individuals to efficiently extract phytoplankton and other suspended particulate matter from the water column, supporting the observed rapid shell growth. The ultimate ash-free dry weight of adult specimens reaches 1.831 g , which represents the total organic biomass accumulated over the animal's lifespan, excluding shell material. This dry weight is achieved through years of sustained feeding activity. The maximum recorded longevity for E. directus under a 12 °C [T = 12 °C] thermal regime is 7 years [am = 7 years], a lifespan that allows for multiple reproductive seasons. The interplay between feeding rate, energy assimilation, and metabolic expenditure ultimately governs the species' life-history schedule.

The early life of Ensis directus begins with a remarkably small starting dimension, as the shell length at birth has been measured at just 0.0136 cm [Lb = 0.0136 cm]. This minute size corresponds to the prodissoconch stage immediately following hatching from the fertilized ovum. The transition from this planktotrophic veliger larva to benthic juvenile involves a dramatic allometric shift that culminates in metamorphic competence and substratum attachment. The considerable growth increments observed throughout the first two years, from the initial larval size of 0.0136 cm [Lb = 0.0136 cm] to the substantial dimensions of 8.0 cm  at 730 days, demonstrate a period of rapid somatic expansion that slows as asymptotic size approaches at a temperature of 12 °C [T = 12 °C]. The total organic mass referenced in the ultimate ash-free dry weight of 1.831 g  is the product of this sustained feeding effort over the species' seven-year lifespan (7 years) [am = 7 years] at a temperature of 12 °C [T = 12 °C]. This life-history configuration, characterised by moderate growth rates, a relatively late age at puberty, and a respectable maximum longevity, positions E. directus as a species well-suited to the dynamic intertidal and shallow subtidal environments it inhabits along Atlantic coastlines.
